h1: Skull and Facial Bones Anatomy: Complete Guide to All 22 Adult Skull Bones
blurb: Complete osteology of all 22 adult skull bones—8 cranial vault bones and 14 facial bones—paired with anterior surface and medial sagittal cutaway views.
lead: Built from twenty-two interlocking bones joined primarily by immovable sutures, the adult human skull forms both an armored vault for the brain and a frame for the face. In this illustrated guide to skull and facial bones anatomy, we examine 30 documented structures—including frontal bone, right maxilla, left maxilla, right zygomatic bone—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Built from twenty-two interlocking bones joined primarily by immovable sutures, the adult human skull forms both an armored vault for the brain and a frame for the face. An adult skull has 22 bones: 14 facial (six paired types and the unpaired vomer and mandible) and 8 cranial. The maxillae anchor upper teeth, the mandible is the mobile lower jaw, and the palatine bones lie deep at the back of the hard palate. Ethmoid contributes to the upper bony nasal septum but is counted as a cranial bone; the inferior nasal conchae are separate paired facial bones. A front view cannot reliably identify every deep or posterior bone; those entries use an unpinned sectional reference. The hyoid and the six ear ossicles belong in the wider 206-bone adult skeleton count but not the 22 skull bones. Within the human body, the skull & facial bones (Ossa cranii et faciei) is situated in head: 8 cranial bones around the brain and 14 facial bones supporting jaws, orbits and nose, receives arterial perfusion via external carotid branches supply much of face; internal carotid/ophthalmic contributions supply orbit and forehead, and is innervated by CN V carries most facial skin sensation; CN VII moves expression muscles; CN V3 moves major chewing muscles.

The frontal bone (Os frontale) forms the forehead, roof of the orbits and much of the anterior cranial floor. Physiologically, the frontal bone protects frontal brain and supports the upper orbit. Structurally, the right maxilla (Maxilla dextra) comprises right upper jaw below the orbit, housing upper-tooth sockets and much of the maxillary sinus. Physiologically, the right maxilla forms upper jaw, orbit floor and anterior hard palate. Structurally, the left maxilla (Maxilla sinistra) comprises left upper jaw below the orbit; meets the opposite maxilla at the anterior midline. Physiologically, the left maxilla holds upper teeth and forms the left anterior hard palate. Structurally, the right zygomatic bone (Os zygomaticum dextrum) comprises right cheekbone forming the lateral rim and part of the floor of the orbit. Physiologically, the right zygomatic bone supports cheek contour and the bony orbit. Structurally, the left zygomatic bone (Os zygomaticum sinistrum) comprises left cheekbone forming the outer orbital rim and meeting the temporal bone at the arch. Physiologically, the left zygomatic bone protects the outer orbit and supports facial shape. The right nasal bone (Os nasale dextrum) is small right bone at the bony bridge of the nose, above the nasal opening. Physiologically, the right nasal bone forms the upper nasal bridge, not the flexible nose tip.

Clinically, regarding the frontal bone, the frontal sinus lies within the bone; fracture patterns can involve the anterior cranial floor. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the right maxilla, the infraorbital nerve (CN V2) exits through its infraorbital foramen. In clinical pathology involving the left maxilla, dental roots and maxillary sinus lie close together. Medical evaluation of the right zygomatic bone also notes that zygomatic fractures may affect the orbital rim and cheek projection.

questions.question: How many facial bones are in an adult human skull?
questions.answer: Fourteen: paired maxillae, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine and inferior nasal concha bones, plus the single vomer and mandible. The adult skull also has eight cranial bones, for 22 skull bones in total. The mandible (Mandibula) is single adult lower jaw consisting of a body and paired ascending rami. Physiologically, the mandible houses lower teeth and moves at the temporomandibular joints for chewing and speech.

questions.question: Which facial bones are easiest to identify from the front?
questions.answer: The maxillae form the upper jaw, the zygomatic bones form the cheeks, the nasal bones form the bony bridge of the nose, and the single mandible forms the lower jaw. Small lacrimal and deep palatine bones cannot reliably be isolated on a simple anterior photograph. The right nasal bone (Os nasale dextrum) is small right bone at the bony bridge of the nose, above the nasal opening. Physiologically, the right nasal bone forms the upper nasal bridge, not the flexible nose tip.

questions.question: Is the inferior nasal concha part of the ethmoid bone?
questions.answer: No. Right and left inferior nasal conchae are independent facial bones. The middle and superior conchae are parts of the ethmoid, which is counted as a cranial bone. Anatomically, the ethmoid bone (Os ethmoidale) lies between the orbits; forms the upper nasal septum, parts of the orbit and nasal roof. Physiologically, the ethmoid bone supports the olfactory region and separates the upper nasal cavity from the cranial cavity.

questions.question: Does the 22-bone skull count include ear ossicles or the hyoid?
questions.answer: No. The six middle-ear ossicles and the single hyoid bone are additional bones associated with the head and neck; they are included separately in the conventional 206-bone adult skeleton count. Structurally, the right parietal bone (Os parietale dextrum) comprises right upper side of the cranial vault; meets the frontal, opposite parietal, occipital and temporal bones. Physiologically, the right parietal bone protects the superior and lateral cerebrum.

questions.question: Which nerve moves the facial-expression muscles around the skull?
questions.answer: Facial nerve CN VII drives most muscles of facial expression after passing through the temporal bone and parotid region. Trigeminal CN V carries most facial skin sensation, and its V3 division supplies the major jaw-closing muscles. Bones and nerves are different structures. Structurally, the right temporal bone (Os temporale dextrum) comprises right lower side and base of the skull, surrounding the external acoustic opening and internal ear spaces. Physiologically, the right temporal bone houses hearing and balance structures; helps form the jaw joint.
